sections.h2: Where do Pulaski County property tax bills come from, and who collects them?
sections.html:
In Pulaski County, the Property Valuation Administrator in Somerset values each parcel, and the Pulaski County Sheriff's tax office sends the bill and collects it. The PVA can be reached at (606) 679-1812. The sheriff keeps a separate tax mailbox, taxes@pulaskisheriff.com, and its office staff work Monday through Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM.

Rates come from the taxing bodies, not from either office. The county, the school district and other taxing districts each add a rate. Three public school systems serve the county (Pulaski County, Somerset Independent and Science Hill Independent), so the school share of a bill depends on where the house sits.

The sheriff collects more than houses. Its FAQ lists real estate with school taxes, tangible property, franchise and gas taxes, undeveloped land, oil, and limestone, sand and gravel.

sections.h2: What is the Pulaski County payment calendar?
sections.html:
According to the sheriff's own FAQ, bills start going out in the first week of October. The schedule below follows that page, and the 5 percent step in January matches KRS 134.015.

Pulaski County sheriff's payment steps for a real estate tax bill
When paidAmount
October 1 to November 1Bill less a 2 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Base amount
January 1 to January 31Base amount plus 5 percent
February 1 to April 15Base amount plus 21 percent
From April 16Pay the County Clerk, (606) 679-2042

The sheriff takes cash, checks and cards at the counter, with a small fee added to card payments. Partial payments are refused: the whole bill must be paid at once. Mailing a payment with a self-addressed stamped envelope earns a receipt, and a lost bill can be reissued free of charge.

sections.h2: What would a typical Pulaski County homeowner owe?
sections.html:
Kentucky's 2025 state real property rate is 10.6 cents per $100 of assessed value. The Census puts the median owner-occupied home in Pulaski County at $166,900, which makes the state's piece about $176.91 for that house. Local rates stack on top, and the total shifts with the school district.

Homeowners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, deduct $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 years. On a $166,900 home that leaves $117,800 taxable, and the state share falls to roughly $124.87. The sheriff's FAQ still quotes an older deduction figure, so rely on the Department of Revenue's amount and confirm with the PVA when you apply.

A 2 percent discount applies to the whole bill if it is paid between October 1 and November 1.

sections.h2: How do I challenge a Pulaski County assessment?
sections.html:
Every appeal in Kentucky begins with a conference at the PVA office, whether the value is for a house on Lake Cumberland or a farm near Eubank. The roll is open for public inspection beginning the first Monday in May for thirteen days. The PVA must walk you through how your number was reached and write down the claimed value, any change agreed and the outcome.

  • File with the county clerk by close of business the day after the inspection period ends.
  • The local board of assessment appeals sits 25 to 35 days after inspection, for up to five days.
  • Bring physical descriptions of the land and buildings, insurance policies, construction costs and sales listings. A board must deny an appeal that arrives without proof.
  • Paid representatives must be attorneys, CPAs, brokers, appraisers or others the statute names, and need written authorization.

If tax bills are printed before the board rules and the final value lands above your claim, the county issues a supplemental bill for the gap.

sections.h2: What if I sell my Pulaski County house in the middle of a tax year?
sections.html:
The sheriff's FAQ answers this directly: whoever owned the property on January 1 owes the tax due in the fall, and it may have been prorated at closing. Ask the closing attorney how the contract splits the year, and ask the tax office for a paid or unpaid status on the parcel.

State law supports the same result. KRS 134.015 calls the tax the owner's personal debt from the assessment date, and a delinquency lien under KRS 134.420 stays with the land for eleven years no matter who buys it. Mortgage companies that escrow tax usually pay the bills they hold, but the sheriff points out that the bill is still the homeowner's responsibility, so send a copy to your lender if your address has changed.

An owner who moves should also tell the PVA, because the homestead deduction follows the person and the new buyer must apply on their own.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Pulaski County taxes after April 15?
sections.html:
On April 16 the sheriff hands unpaid bills to the County Clerk, and each becomes a certificate of delinquency with a lien on the parcel. The sheriff's FAQ notes that a buyer of a delinquent bill holds the lien and can collect the tax plus 12 percent per year and expenses such as attorney and filing fees. The property itself is not auctioned at this stage.

The clerk adds interest at 1 percent a month. The Department of Revenue's examples show a $1,000 bill becoming $1,254 at transfer and about $1,387.79 within five business days, with the county attorney's commission and postage adding more once notices go out. A county attorney 30-day notice and, if needed, a 60-day notice precede the sale, which must come 90 to 135 days after the transfer.

Delinquent lists are published by the clerk, and paying the clerk before the sale stops a third party from buying the bill.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Pulaski County, Kentucky?
sections.html:
Pulaski County was created in December 1798 from land of Lincoln and Green counties and is named for Casimir Pulaski. Somerset is the seat, and Burnside, Eubank, Ferguson and Science Hill are the other cities. At about 658 square miles of land, it is the third-largest county in the state, and Lake Cumberland, known for houseboating, anchors the south. Pulaski County is dry except for Somerset and Burnside.

Getting around is easy by Kentucky standards. US 27 runs north to south, Kentucky 80 east to west, and the eastern end of the Cumberland Expressway meets US 27 north of Somerset. A loop, Kentucky 914, circles the city. Interstate 75 is about 28 miles east, and Lexington is 76 miles north. Somerset Community College has a campus on Monticello Street, and the Lake Cumberland Regional Airport sits at the south end of Somerset.

  • 2025 population estimate: 67,384, up 3.6 percent since 2020.
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 72.5 percent, among 26,210 households.
  • Median home value: $166,900; median gross rent: $803.
  • Median household income: $51,898; poverty rate 20.1 percent.
  • Building permits in 2025: 129.

A house with a roof, septic or lakefront issue can sell as-is for cash, and the outstanding tax is paid from the proceeds at closing.

faqs.q: How do I pay my Pulaski County property taxes?
faqs.a: Pay the Pulaski County Sheriff's tax office by mail or at the counter with cash, check, or a card that carries a small fee. Taxes must be paid in full, since partial payments are not taken.

faqs.q: What penalty applies in Pulaski County after January?
faqs.a: Five percent for payments made January 1 through January 31, and 21 percent from February 1 through April 15, according to the sheriff's FAQ. After April 15 the bill moves to the County Clerk.

faqs.q: Is there a discount for early payment in Pulaski County?
faqs.a: Yes, 2 percent. It applies to a bill paid from October 1 through November 1, and the base amount is due from November 2 through December 31.

faqs.q: Who do I call about the homestead exemption in Pulaski County?
faqs.a: Call the Property Valuation Administrator at (606) 679-1812. The Department of Revenue set the deduction at $49,100 for 2025 and 2026 for owners 65 or older or totally disabled.

faqs.q: Can the sheriff sell my house for unpaid taxes in Pulaski County?
faqs.a: Not directly. Unpaid bills go to the County Clerk after April 15, and the delinquent bill is sold to a third party who holds a lien on the property, with 12 percent yearly interest and costs.
